appearance.organs.leaf.insertion.why: A peltate blade is drawn on its own petiole, held flat across the petiole's tip, centred on it where the petiole meets the blade underneath; an epeltate one goes on from its petiole in one card.

appearance.organs.leaf.hairs.density.why: How much of a blade's face its hairs hide, from the words floras use (Harris and Harris): none on a glabrous blade, a little where they are few or soon lost, about a third where they are minute or sparse and long, half where they are stiff, most where they are shaggy or silky, nearly all under a felt or a wool.

appearance.organs.leaf.hairs.lie.why: How a blade's hairs stand: pressed flat toward its tip where they are strigose or silky, matted low in a felt or a wool, spreading where they are soft, and straight out where they are stiff or bristly.

appearance.organs.leaf.hairs.curl.why: How a blade's hairs bend: straight where they are stiff, pressed flat or minute, a little wavy where they are soft, shaggy where they are villous, curled and tangled in a felt or a wool.

appearance.organs.leaf.hairs.length.why: A blade's hairs are as long as its words make them where no length is stated (Harris and Harris): a tenth of a millimetre or two where minute, about half a millimetre where short and soft or felted, one to two where long, stiff or silky, two or three where shaggy or woolly. A length a flora states (leaf_hair_length_m) wins over the word's.

appearance.organs.leaf.shape.round.why: Serrate teeth are saw teeth pointing to the tip; dentate teeth point outward, so they are drawn blunter and more upright; crenate teeth are rounded scallops.

appearance.defaults.note: How PlantGen draws an organ its taxa say nothing about, a choice of the model's (visual forms Skill 1, 2026-10-14): each organ kind on the card the generator gives it by default, so that every organ a program grows has a look and every rule on the taxa's characters reaches it.

generator.defaults.dioecious.note: How PlantGen draws the sexes, a choice of the model's (dioecy, 2026-10-14): a plant bears both sexes, unless its taxa state it dioecious.

generator.defaults.sex.note: How PlantGen draws the sexes, a choice of the model's (dioecy, 2026-10-14): a plant's sex is its own draw, dealt across a package's seeds so that both sexes grow; the typical plant (sex 0.5) is female, so it shows its fruit.

rules.appearance.organs.leaf.shape.width.note: Each word's width over length lies inside the band the Systematics Association's chart of plane shapes gives it, the value in the band the model's choice: lanceolate and oblanceolate 3:1 to 6:1 (0.25); elliptic, ovate and obovate 3:2 to 2:1 (0.57, 0.6, 0.6); orbicular about 1:1 (0.95); linear longer than 6:1, its sides parallel (0.08). The chart gives oblong and spatulate by their sides, not a band: 0.4 and 0.35 are the model's. A flora's two words ("ovate to lanceolate") read as the forms between them, so the width is their middle. Where a flora measures the blade (or leaflet), its width over its length, the middle of each range, comes first (visual forms leaf blades, 2026-10-15), as Asteraceae has done since its family rule.

rules.appearance.organs.leaf.shape.leafl.note: A compound leaf's shape word describes its leaflets, so a leaflet's width follows the same chart as a blade's. Each word's width over length lies inside the band the Systematics Association's chart of plane shapes gives it, the value in the band the model's choice: lanceolate and oblanceolate 3:1 to 6:1 (0.25); elliptic, ovate and obovate 3:2 to 2:1 (0.57, 0.6, 0.6); orbicular about 1:1 (0.95); linear longer than 6:1, its sides parallel (0.08). The chart gives oblong and spatulate by their sides, not a band: 0.4 and 0.35 are the model's. A flora's two words ("ovate to lanceolate") read as the forms between them, so the width is their middle. Where a flora measures the blade (or leaflet), its width over its length, the middle of each range, comes first (visual forms leaf blades, 2026-10-15), as Asteraceae has done since its family rule.

rules.appearance.organs.leaf.shape.outli.note: Outlines drawn to the Systematics Association chart's definitions: lanceolate and ovate widest below the middle, oblanceolate and obovate above it, elliptic and orbicular at it, linear and oblong with their sides parallel, spatulate a broad rounded tip on a long narrow base. The curves are the model's, each the half-width as a share of the widest at 15 places from the base (u 0) to the tip (1), the same places for every word, so two words that tie draw the outline halfway between theirs. An ellipse for elliptic and orbicular, a rounded rectangle (a superellipse of power 4) for oblong. A compound leaf's word is its leaflets' (spec rework P4).

rules.appearance.organs.leaf.insertion.note: Kaplan (2022, pp. 426 and 442-444, Fig. 17.15): most blades are epeltate, the petiole meeting the blade at its basal margin; a peltate blade has the petiole joined on its underside, inside its outline, like an umbrella, and is held near horizontal on the petiole; a latently peltate blade is held so but the petiole still meets its margin. Many digitate leaves are peltate in organisation: with only lateral pairs beside the terminal leaflet the ring of leaflets is open toward the stem (latent), and an extra cross leaflet opposite the terminal one closes it (manifest), as in Lupinus polyphyllus. How PlantGen draws it, a choice of the model's (visual forms leaf blades, 2026-10-15): a blade that is not epeltate on a petiole of its own, its card turned level about where it meets the petiole.

rules.appearance.organs.leaf.hairs.densi.note: The hair words are the botanical glossary's (Harris and Harris, Plant Identification Terminology): glabrous without hairs, glabrescent nearly so or losing them, puberulent minutely hairy, pubescent with short soft hairs, strigose with stiff hairs pressed flat, sericeous silky with long hairs pressed flat, pilose with long soft sparse hairs, villous with long soft shaggy hairs, hirsute with stiff spreading hairs, crisped with curled or kinked hairs, hispid bristly, tomentose with a felt of matted curled hairs, lanate woolly. How much of the face each word's hairs hide is the model's choice, set by eye against iNaturalist photographs of Asarum, Aristolochia and other hairy blades (2026-10-16), and rising from the bare to the felted words.

The lengths, from a tenth of a millimetre for minute hairs to a few millimetres for shaggy or woolly ones, are the model's estimates for each word where a flora gives no length. Where a flora states their length (leaf_hair_length_m), that is the drawn one.

rules.appearance.organs.basal.hairs.edge.note: A ciliate blade is one whose margin is fringed with hairs (Harris and Harris). How thickly the fringe is drawn is the model's choice.

rules.appearance.organs.leaf.hairs_benea.note: A blade's underside is named in the same words as its upper side (a flora's 'abaxially appressed-hirsute', 'surfaces abaxially tomentose') and drawn by the same numbers. The hair words are the botanical glossary's (Harris and Harris, Plant Identification Terminology): glabrous without hairs, glabrescent nearly so or losing them, puberulent minutely hairy, pubescent with short soft hairs, strigose with stiff hairs pressed flat, sericeous silky with long hairs pressed flat, pilose with long soft sparse hairs, villous with long soft shaggy hairs, hirsute with stiff spreading hairs, crisped with curled or kinked hairs, hispid bristly, tomentose with a felt of matted curled hairs, lanate woolly. How much of the face each word's hairs hide is the model's choice, set by eye against iNaturalist photographs of Asarum, Aristolochia and other hairy blades (2026-10-16), and rising from the bare to the felted words.

rules.appearance.organs.leaf.shape.teeth.note: How PlantGen draws a stated leaf margin, a choice of the model's (visual forms, 2026-10-16), the words as the trait defines them: serrate teeth point forward, dentate outward, crenate are rounded, spiny end in spines. The counts and depths are calibrated on the curated species whose leaves are drawn toothed (25 simple and sprig leaves: 2 to 18 teeth a side, about 9 in the middle; tooth depth about 0.03 of the blade's length in the middle; Garry oak's rounded lobes 0.8 round, tanoak's teeth 0.3). A species' own drawn teeth win over these.
